title: Tissues, Skeleton & Muscles
description: Anatomical terms, planes and cavities, tissue types, the integumentary system, bone structure and remodeling, the skeleton and joints, muscle anatomy, contraction physiology and major muscles.

cards.title: In anatomical position, which directional term means closer to a limb's attachment to the trunk (for example, the elbow relative to the wrist)?
cards.body:
Proximal

The opposite is **distal**, meaning farther from the attachment point. These terms are used mainly for limbs and for structures such as tubules.

Example: the elbow is proximal to the wrist; the wrist is distal to the elbow.
Watch out: do not confuse with superior/inferior, which describe position along the whole body axis.
cards.searchQuery: proximal distal anatomical directional terms limb

cards.title: Which directional term means toward or at the body surface, as in the skin relative to the muscles beneath it?
cards.body:
Superficial

The opposite is **deep**, meaning farther from the body surface. The skin is superficial to the skeletal muscles, and the bones are deep to the muscles.

Tip: superficial/deep describe depth, while anterior/posterior describe front/back.
cards.searchQuery: superficial deep anatomical directional terms

cards.title: Which plane of section divides the body or an organ into right and left parts?
cards.body:
Sagittal plane

A sagittal plane runs vertically from front to back. If it passes exactly through the midline and gives equal halves it is the **midsagittal (median)** plane; if off-center it is **parasagittal**.

Tip: a sagittal section shows the profile of the spinal column and the nasal septum edge-on.
cards.searchQuery: sagittal plane divides body left and right

cards.title: Which plane of section divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) parts?
cards.body:
Frontal (coronal) plane

It runs vertically, perpendicular to a sagittal plane. A frontal section of the head separates the face from the back of the skull.

Mnemonic: a **coronal** plane follows where a crown (corona) would sit, side to side across the head.
cards.searchQuery: frontal coronal plane anterior posterior

cards.title: Which plane of section cuts the body horizontally into superior and inferior parts?
cards.body:
Transverse (horizontal) plane

It is perpendicular to the long axis of the body, so the result is a **cross section**. CT and MRI slices through the abdomen are usually transverse.

Watch out: a transverse cut across a long organ gives a cross section, while a cut along its length is a longitudinal section.
cards.searchQuery: transverse horizontal plane cross section

cards.title: Which dome-shaped skeletal muscle separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
cards.body:
The diaphragm

The diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominopelvic cavity. It is the main muscle of quiet inspiration and is innervated by the **phrenic nerve**.

Key idea: the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities together make up the ventral body cavity.
cards.searchQuery: diaphragm separates thoracic and abdominopelvic cavity

cards.title: What is the name of the central partition of the thoracic cavity that contains the heart, thymus, trachea and esophagus, between the two pleural cavities?
cards.body:
Mediastinum

The mediastinum lies between the two lungs. The heart sits within its own **pericardial cavity** inside the mediastinum.

Watch out: the lungs are not in the mediastinum; each lung is in its own pleural cavity.
cards.searchQuery: mediastinum thoracic cavity contents

cards.title: A serous membrane has two layers separated by serous fluid. Which layer covers the surface of an organ?
cards.body:
The visceral layer

The **parietal layer** lines the wall of the body cavity. Serous fluid between the layers reduces friction as organs move.

Example: the heart is covered by visceral pericardium (epicardium), and the pericardial sac lined by parietal pericardium surrounds it.
Mnemonic: **v**isceral = **v**iscera (organs).
cards.searchQuery: serous membrane visceral parietal layer

cards.title: In which abdominopelvic quadrant is the appendix typically found?
cards.body:
Right lower quadrant (RLQ)

The appendix attaches to the cecum, at the start of the large intestine. Appendicitis classically causes pain that shifts to the RLQ. The cecum and ascending colon are also in the RLQ.

Tip: the four quadrants are named from the patient's perspective, not the examiner's.
cards.searchQuery: appendix location right lower quadrant abdomen

cards.title: What is the correct order of structural organization from simplest to most complex?
cards.body:
Chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system, organism

Atoms form molecules (chemical level), molecules form **cells**, similar cells form **tissues**, tissues form **organs**, organs cooperate as **organ systems**, and all systems make up the organism.

Example: cardiac muscle cells form cardiac muscle tissue, which with other tissues forms the heart, part of the cardiovascular system.
cards.searchQuery: levels of structural organization human body

cards.title: What is the anatomical name for the anterior surface of the elbow, where blood is often drawn?
cards.body:
Antecubital region

The **cubital** fossa lies here, and the median cubital vein crosses it. The back of the elbow is the olecranal region.

Tip: the posterior surface of the knee is the **popliteal** region.
cards.searchQuery: antecubital region anterior elbow

cards.title: Are the kidneys intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal?
cards.body:
Retroperitoneal

The kidneys lie behind (posterior to) the parietal peritoneum, against the posterior abdominal wall. Other retroperitoneal organs include the adrenal glands, ureters, most of the pancreas and parts of the duodenum.

Watch out: the stomach, liver and most of the small intestine are intraperitoneal (covered by peritoneum).
cards.searchQuery: kidneys retroperitoneal position

cards.title: Name the four primary tissue types.
cards.body:
Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue

- **Epithelial**: covers surfaces and lines cavities; forms glands.
- **Connective**: supports, binds and protects; has abundant matrix.
- **Muscle**: contracts to produce movement.
- **Nervous**: conducts electrical signals.

Key idea: connective tissue is distinguished by cells scattered in an extracellular matrix; epithelium by tightly packed cells with little matrix.
cards.searchQuery: four primary tissue types epithelial connective muscle nervous

cards.title: Which epithelium, a single layer of flat cells, lines the alveoli and the walls of capillaries, where diffusion is needed?
cards.body:
Simple squamous epithelium

The thin cells give a short diffusion distance. When lining blood vessels and the heart it is called **endothelium**; when lining serous cavities it is called **mesothelium**.

Watch out: do not confuse with stratified squamous, which is thick and protective.
cards.searchQuery: simple squamous epithelium location function

cards.title: Which epithelium lines the stomach and intestines and often contains goblet cells and microvilli for absorption and secretion?
cards.body:
Simple columnar epithelium

Tall cells with nuclei near the base form one layer. In the small intestine the apical **microvilli** increase surface area; **goblet cells** secrete mucus.

Example: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lines the uterine tubes, where cilia move the oocyte along.
cards.searchQuery: simple columnar epithelium stomach intestine goblet

cards.title: Which epithelium lines the trachea, appears layered because nuclei sit at different heights, yet every cell touches the basement membrane?
cards.body:
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium

It contains goblet cells; mucus traps particles and cilia sweep it upward (the **mucociliary escalator**).

Watch out: "pseudo" means false. It is a single layer even though it looks stratified.
cards.searchQuery: pseudostratified ciliated columnar trachea

cards.title: Which epithelium forms the epidermis and lines the esophagus, vagina and mouth, resisting abrasion?
cards.body:
Stratified squamous epithelium

The epidermis is **keratinized** (dead surface cells filled with keratin), while moist linings (mouth, esophagus, vagina) are **nonkeratinized**.

Key idea: the tissue is named for its surface layer of cells, which are squamous here.
cards.searchQuery: stratified squamous epithelium keratinized nonkeratinized

cards.title: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and ureters and can change shape as the organ stretches?
cards.body:
Transitional epithelium (urothelium)

Surface cells look rounded (dome-shaped) when the organ is relaxed and flatten when it is distended, allowing stretch without tearing.

Tip: it is found only in the urinary tract, from renal pelvis to part of the urethra.
cards.searchQuery: transitional epithelium urothelium bladder

cards.title: Which mode of gland secretion releases product by rupture and death of the whole secretory cell, as in sebaceous glands?
cards.body:
Holocrine secretion

In **merocrine** secretion (most sweat and salivary glands) vesicles release product by exocytosis and the cell survives.

Example: sebum from sebaceous glands is holocrine.
cards.searchQuery: holocrine merocrine apocrine gland secretion sebaceous

cards.title: Which cell junction forms a seal between adjacent epithelial cells, preventing leakage of substances between cells?
cards.body:
Tight junction

Tight junctions (zonula occludens) encircle the apical end of the cells. They are essential in the intestinal lining and in the blood-brain barrier.

Watch out: desmosomes anchor cells mechanically (like spot welds), and gap junctions allow small molecules and ions to pass between cells.
cards.searchQuery: tight junction epithelium zonula occludens

cards.title: Which cell of connective tissue proper secretes the fibers and ground substance of the matrix?
cards.body:
Fibroblast

Fibroblasts make collagen, elastin and ground substance, and they migrate into wounds to build scar tissue.

In bone and cartilage the equivalent matrix-building cells are **osteoblasts** and **chondroblasts**.

Tip: the "-blast" suffix means a cell that builds matrix; "-cyte" means the mature, maintaining cell.
cards.searchQuery: fibroblast connective tissue proper matrix

cards.title: Which fiber type is the most abundant protein in the body and gives connective tissue great tensile strength?
cards.body:
Collagen fibers

Collagen resists pulling (tension) but not compression. Tendons, ligaments, the dermis and the organic part of bone are rich in it.

Watch out: **elastic fibers** allow stretch and recoil; **reticular fibers** form a fine supportive network in organs such as the spleen and lymph nodes.
cards.searchQuery: collagen fibers tensile strength connective tissue

cards.title: Which protein of connective tissue fibers lets the walls of large arteries and the lungs stretch and then recoil?
cards.body:
Elastin

Elastic fibers (elastin) stretch to one and a half times their length and snap back. They are abundant in large arteries, the vocal cords and lung tissue.

Example: elastic recoil of the aorta keeps blood moving forward during diastole.
cards.searchQuery: elastin elastic fibers arteries recoil

cards.title: Which loose connective tissue serves as the body's "packing material", lying beneath epithelia and around vessels, nerves and organs?
cards.body:
Areolar connective tissue

It has all three fiber types in a gel-like matrix, holds tissue fluid (so it swells in edema), and houses defense cells such as macrophages and mast cells.

Key idea: areolar is the most widely distributed connective tissue proper; it forms the lamina propria of mucous membranes.
cards.searchQuery: areolar loose connective tissue location function

cards.title: Which connective tissue, composed of cells with a large lipid droplet pushing the nucleus aside, stores energy and insulates?
cards.body:
Adipose tissue

Besides energy storage, adipose tissue insulates, cushions organs (kidneys, eyes) and secretes hormones such as leptin. It is a type of loose connective tissue.

Watch out: **brown fat** is rich in mitochondria and generates heat rather than just storing energy.
cards.searchQuery: adipose tissue function lipid storage

cards.title: Which tissue, with densely packed parallel collagen bundles and few cells, forms tendons and ligaments?
cards.body:
Dense regular connective tissue

The parallel fibers resist tension in one direction. Tendons attach muscle to bone, and ligaments connect bone to bone.

Watch out: its blood supply is poor, so tendon and ligament injuries heal slowly.
Mnemonic: **T**endons connect **T**issue (muscle) to bone; **L**igaments connect bone to bone, like **L**inking.
cards.searchQuery: dense regular connective tissue tendons ligaments

cards.title: Which tissue, with collagen bundles running in many directions, forms the dermis and the capsules around organs and joints?
cards.body:
Dense irregular connective tissue

Because the fibers run in random directions, it withstands tension from many directions.

Example: the deep (reticular) layer of the dermis, the periosteum, and the fibrous capsule of the kidney are dense irregular tissue.
cards.searchQuery: dense irregular connective tissue dermis capsule

cards.title: Which is the most abundant cartilage, found at articular surfaces, costal cartilages, the nose and tracheal rings?
cards.body:
Hyaline cartilage

Its glassy matrix has fine collagen fibers. It also forms the embryonic skeleton and the **epiphyseal plate** in growing bones.

Key idea: hyaline cartilage supports and reinforces while giving slight flexibility and a smooth, low-friction surface.
cards.searchQuery: hyaline cartilage location articular costal

cards.title: Which cartilage, rich in thick collagen fibers, resists compression and tension in the intervertebral discs, menisci and pubic symphysis?
cards.body:
Fibrocartilage

It is the strongest cartilage and acts as a shock absorber.

Example: the **annulus fibrosus** of an intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage, and tearing a knee meniscus damages fibrocartilage.
cards.searchQuery: fibrocartilage intervertebral disc meniscus

cards.title: Which cartilage, rich in elastic fibers, forms the external ear (pinna) and the epiglottis?
cards.body:
Elastic cartilage

It tolerates repeated bending and returns to its shape. The epiglottis flips over the larynx during swallowing.

Tip: link the three cartilages by location: hyaline (joints, ribs, trachea), fibro (discs, menisci) and elastic (ear, epiglottis).
cards.searchQuery: elastic cartilage ear epiglottis

cards.title: Why does cartilage heal slowly after injury?
cards.body:
It is avascular

Cartilage has no blood vessels. Chondrocytes in lacunae receive nutrients and oxygen by **diffusion** through the matrix from the perichondrium or synovial fluid.

Watch out: the same absence of blood vessels is true of epithelium, which is nourished from the connective tissue beneath it.
Key idea: poor blood supply means slow repair for cartilage, tendon and ligament injuries.
cards.searchQuery: why cartilage heals slowly avascular chondrocytes

cards.title: Blood is classified as which of the four primary tissue types?
cards.body:
Connective tissue

Blood has living cells (erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets) in a fluid matrix, the **plasma**. Like other connective tissues it derives from mesenchyme.

Key idea: a connective tissue is defined by its cells in an extracellular matrix, not by being solid.
cards.searchQuery: blood classified as connective tissue matrix plasma

cards.title: What general name is given to the supporting, non-conducting cells of nervous tissue?
cards.body:
Neuroglia (glial cells)

Glia support, insulate and nourish neurons. Examples include astrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes in the CNS, and Schwann cells and satellite cells in the PNS.

Key idea: neurons conduct impulses, while neuroglia support the neurons and outnumber them.
cards.searchQuery: neuroglia glial cells nervous tissue

cards.title: Which type of membrane lines freely movable joint cavities and secretes lubricating synovial fluid, with no epithelium?
cards.body:
Synovial membrane

It is made of connective tissue only (areolar with some adipose). Its fluid lubricates the joint and nourishes the articular cartilage.

Watch out: serous and mucous membranes both contain an epithelium; synovial membranes are the one membrane type that does not.
cards.searchQuery: synovial membrane connective tissue joint cavity

cards.title: Which membrane type lines body cavities that open to the exterior, such as the digestive, respiratory and urinary tracts?
cards.body:
Mucous membrane (mucosa)

It has an epithelial layer over a loose connective tissue layer, the **lamina propria**. Many mucosae secrete mucus, but not all (the lining of the urinary tract does not).

Watch out: serous membranes line closed ventral cavities and secrete serous fluid, not mucus.
cards.searchQuery: mucous membrane mucosa lamina propria

cards.title: What is the term for the replacement of damaged tissue with dense connective (scar) tissue during repair?
cards.body:
Fibrosis

When a tissue cannot regenerate, fibroblasts fill the defect with collagen, forming a **scar**. Scar tissue is strong but lacks the function of the original tissue.

Example: after a heart attack, necrotic cardiac muscle is replaced by scar, because cardiac muscle regenerates poorly.
cards.searchQuery: fibrosis scar tissue tissue repair

cards.title: During tissue repair, what is the delicate, pink, new tissue made of capillary buds and fibroblasts called?
cards.body:
Granulation tissue

It forms in the organization phase of healing, bringing blood supply and fibroblasts into the clot. It later matures into scar tissue.

Watch out: excess granulation tissue (proud flesh) can impede epithelial regrowth.
cards.searchQuery: granulation tissue wound healing capillaries fibroblasts

cards.title: What are the four cardinal signs of acute inflammation?
cards.body:
Redness, heat, swelling and pain

Latin: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor. They come from vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and chemical mediators such as histamine and prostaglandins.

Tip: loss of function is sometimes listed as a fifth sign.
Watch out: the swelling is edema from fluid leaving the capillaries, not new tissue growth.
cards.searchQuery: four cardinal signs of inflammation redness heat swelling pain

cards.title: Epithelial tissue is richly innervated but lacks which structure, so it relies on diffusion from underlying connective tissue?
cards.body:
Blood vessels (it is avascular)

Epithelial cells lie on a **basement membrane** and are nourished from capillaries in the connective tissue beneath. Epithelium regenerates quickly.

Example: skin and gut lining cells are replaced continuously.
Key idea: avascular but innervated; the opposite of what many students assume.
cards.searchQuery: epithelium avascular innervated basement membrane diffusion

cards.title: Which cell junction contains connexons, channels that let ions and small molecules pass directly between cells?
cards.body:
Gap junction

Adjacent cells' connexons align to form a pore. In heart muscle and smooth muscle, gap junctions let action potentials spread from cell to cell.

Watch out: tight junctions seal, desmosomes anchor, and gap junctions communicate.
cards.searchQuery: gap junction connexons cell communication

cards.title: List the five epidermal layers of thick skin from the surface down to the deepest.
cards.body:
Corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, basale

The **stratum lucidum** is present only in thick skin (palms and soles). Cells move upward from the basale, flatten, fill with keratin and die as they reach the corneum.

Mnemonic: "**C**ome, **L**et's **G**et **S**un **B**urned" (surface to deep).
cards.searchQuery: epidermis five layers stratum corneum lucidum granulosum spinosum basale

cards.title: Which is the deepest layer of the epidermis, where stem cells divide to replace keratinocytes (and where melanocytes sit)?
cards.body:
Stratum basale

Also called the stratum germinativum. It lies on the basement membrane above the dermis and contains dividing keratinocyte stem cells, melanocytes and Merkel (tactile) cells.

Key idea: the epidermis is renewed from the bottom up, so cells in the stratum corneum are the oldest.
cards.searchQuery: stratum basale deepest epidermis stem cells

cards.title: Which epidermal cell makes the pigment melanin, packages it in melanosomes and passes it to keratinocytes?
cards.body:
Melanocyte

Melanin forms a protective cap over the nuclei of keratinocytes, shielding DNA from ultraviolet damage. Skin color differences depend mainly on the amount and type of melanin made, not on the number of melanocytes.

Watch out: keratinocytes are the most numerous epidermal cells; melanocytes produce the pigment.
cards.searchQuery: melanocyte melanin melanosomes epidermis

cards.title: Which layer of the dermis, made of areolar connective tissue, pushes up into the epidermis as dermal papillae and produces fingerprints?
cards.body:
Papillary layer

The papillary layer sits just under the epidermis and contains capillaries and touch receptors. The pattern of its dermal papillae forms **friction ridges**, the fingerprints.

Watch out: the deeper **reticular layer** is dense irregular connective tissue and makes up about 80% of the dermis.
cards.searchQuery: papillary layer dermis dermal papillae fingerprints

cards.title: Which layer beneath the dermis, mostly adipose tissue, anchors the skin and insulates, but is not technically part of the skin?
cards.body:
Hypodermis

Also called the subcutaneous layer or superficial fascia. It stores fat, insulates against heat loss and is the site of subcutaneous injections.

Tip: the skin (cutaneous membrane) = epidermis + dermis only.
cards.searchQuery: hypodermis subcutaneous layer superficial fascia

cards.title: Using the adult rule of nines, what percentage of total body surface area is one entire lower limb (front and back)? Give the number only.
cards.body:
18

Adult rule of nines: head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each lower limb 18%, perineum 1%.

Example: a burn covering the whole anterior trunk and one arm is about $18\% + 9\% = 27\%$ of body surface.
Watch out: children have proportionally larger heads, so the rule is adjusted for them.
cards.searchQuery: rule of nines burn body surface area lower limb

cards.title: Which is the most common type of skin cancer, arising from stratum basale cells and rarely metastasizing?
cards.body:
Basal cell carcinoma

It is strongly linked to sun exposure and often appears as a pearly nodule with a central ulcer.

Watch out: **melanoma**, from melanocytes, is much less common but the most dangerous because it metastasizes early. **Squamous cell carcinoma** arises from stratum spinosum keratinocytes.
cards.searchQuery: basal cell carcinoma most common skin cancer

cards.title: Skin exposed to ultraviolet B radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into a precursor of which vitamin?
cards.body:
Vitamin D (cholecalciferol, D3)

The liver then adds a hydroxyl group and the kidney makes the active form, **calcitriol**, which raises intestinal absorption of $\ce{Ca^2+}$.

Example: vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets, with soft, bowed bones.
cards.searchQuery: skin vitamin D synthesis 7-dehydrocholesterol UVB

cards.title: What is the structural unit of compact bone, made of concentric lamellae around a central canal?
cards.body:
Osteon (Haversian system)

The central canal carries blood vessels and nerves, and osteocytes sit in **lacunae** between the rings of lamellae.

Key idea: the osteon runs parallel to the long axis of the bone, giving resistance to stress along that direction.
cards.searchQuery: osteon Haversian system compact bone

cards.title: Which canals run perpendicular to the long axis of a bone, linking central canals with the periosteum and marrow cavity?
cards.body:
Perforating (Volkmann's) canals

They carry vessels and nerves across osteons. The **central (Haversian) canals** run lengthwise.

Mnemonic: **V**olkmann's canals run **v**ertical to the Haversian canals' length (perpendicular).
cards.searchQuery: perforating Volkmann canals bone

cards.title: What are the tiny channels in bone matrix that connect neighboring lacunae and let osteocytes exchange nutrients and wastes?
cards.body:
Canaliculi

Osteocyte processes extend through the canaliculi and contact one another via gap junctions, so cells deep in the hard matrix still reach blood vessels in the central canal.

Watch out: lacunae are the small chambers holding the osteocytes; canaliculi are the thin tunnels between them.
cards.searchQuery: bone canaliculi lacunae osteocytes

cards.title: Which large multinucleated bone cell, derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage, resorbs bone matrix with acid and enzymes?
cards.body:
Osteoclast

An osteoclast attaches to bone and forms a **ruffled border**, secreting acid and lysosomal enzymes into a sealed pocket that dissolves mineral and matrix, releasing $\ce{Ca^2+}$.

Mnemonic: osteo**c**last **c**hews bone; osteo**b**last **b**uilds it.
cards.searchQuery: osteoclast bone resorption ruffled border

cards.title: Which bone cell secretes osteoid, the organic matrix of bone, and promotes its mineralization?
cards.body:
Osteoblast

Osteoblasts lay down collagen-rich osteoid and promote mineral deposition. Once surrounded by their own matrix they become **osteocytes**, the mature cells that maintain the bone.

Key idea: osteoblasts build, osteocytes maintain and osteoclasts resorb.
cards.searchQuery: osteoblast osteoid bone formation

cards.title: Which calcium phosphate mineral crystal gives bone its hardness and compressive strength?
cards.body:
Hydroxyapatite

The inorganic matrix (about two-thirds of bone by weight) is hydroxyapatite, while the organic matrix (collagen) provides tensile strength and flexibility.

Watch out: without collagen, bone would be brittle; without mineral, it would be flexible like rubber.
cards.searchQuery: hydroxyapatite bone mineral calcium phosphate

cards.title: What is the name of the shaft of a long bone?
cards.body:
Diaphysis

It is a tube of compact bone surrounding the **medullary cavity**, which contains yellow marrow (fat) in adults. The ends are the **epiphyses**, mostly spongy bone covered by articular cartilage.

Tip: **dia** sounds like "through"; the diaphysis is the long middle section.
cards.searchQuery: diaphysis shaft long bone medullary cavity

cards.title: Which layer of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis allows long bones to lengthen during growth?
cards.body:
Epiphyseal plate (growth plate)

Chondrocytes divide on the epiphyseal side and the cartilage is replaced by bone on the diaphyseal side. At the end of puberty, the plate ossifies, leaving the **epiphyseal line**.

Watch out: appositional growth (widening) happens at the periosteum and is independent of this plate.
cards.searchQuery: epiphyseal plate growth plate long bone growth

cards.title: Which dense connective tissue membrane covers the outer surface of bone, except at joint surfaces, and anchors tendons with Sharpey's fibers?
cards.body:
Periosteum

It has an outer fibrous layer and an inner osteogenic layer containing osteoblasts. Nerves and vessels enter bone through it, which is why a bone bruise is painful.

Watch out: the **endosteum** lines the medullary cavity and the trabeculae inside the bone.
cards.searchQuery: periosteum bone outer membrane Sharpey fibers

cards.title: Which type of bone formation replaces a hyaline cartilage model and forms most of the skeleton, including long bones?
cards.body:
Endochondral ossification

A cartilage model is invaded by blood vessels and osteoblasts, producing a **primary ossification center** in the diaphysis, then secondary centers in the epiphyses.

Watch out: **intramembranous ossification** forms flat bones of the skull and most of the clavicle directly from mesenchyme, with no cartilage model.
cards.searchQuery: endochondral ossification cartilage model long bones

cards.title: Which principle states that bone grows and remodels in response to the mechanical stresses placed on it?
cards.body:
Wolff's law

Bone is added where stress is high and removed where it is low. Weight-bearing exercise increases bone density, while prolonged bed rest or spaceflight decreases it.

Example: a tennis player's racket arm has denser bone than the other arm.
cards.searchQuery: Wolff's law bone remodeling mechanical stress

cards.title: What bone disease, common in postmenopausal women after estrogen falls, results from resorption outpacing formation and low bone mass?
cards.body:
Osteoporosis

Bone mass and trabecular structure decline, raising fracture risk, especially in the vertebrae, hip and wrist. Prevention includes calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise.

Watch out: **osteomalacia** (adult) and **rickets** (child) result from poor mineralization, not from loss of bone matrix.
cards.searchQuery: osteoporosis low bone mass postmenopausal

cards.title: Which division of the skeleton includes the bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles?
cards.body:
Appendicular skeleton

It has 126 bones. The **axial skeleton** (80 bones) includes the skull, hyoid, auditory ossicles, vertebral column and thoracic cage.

Watch out: the girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton, but the sacrum (part of the vertebral column) is axial.
cards.searchQuery: appendicular skeleton axial skeleton division bones

cards.title: Which suture joins the two parietal bones along the midline of the skull's roof?
cards.body:
Sagittal suture

The other major sutures: **coronal** (frontal bone and parietals), **lambdoid** (parietals and occipital) and **squamous** (temporal and parietal).

Tip: sutures are fibrous joints (synarthroses) that permit no movement in adults.
cards.searchQuery: sagittal suture parietal bones skull

cards.title: Which skull bone contains the foramen magnum, through which the spinal cord joins the brainstem?
cards.body:
Occipital bone

The occipital condyles on either side of the foramen magnum articulate with the first cervical vertebra (the atlas).

Key idea: the occipital bone forms the posterior and inferior part of the cranium.
cards.searchQuery: foramen magnum occipital bone

cards.title: Which bat-shaped bone forms part of the cranial floor and has a saddle-like depression (sella turcica) that holds the pituitary gland?
cards.body:
Sphenoid bone

The sphenoid articulates with all other cranial bones, so it acts like a keystone. The pituitary sits in the **hypophyseal fossa** of the sella turcica.

Watch out: the optic canal and foramen rotundum are also in the sphenoid; the cribriform plate is in the ethmoid.
cards.searchQuery: sphenoid bone sella turcica pituitary

cards.title: Which skull bone has a cribriform plate, perforated for olfactory nerve fibers, and a crista galli?
cards.body:
Ethmoid bone

The ethmoid lies between the orbits and forms part of the nasal septum and the roof of the nasal cavity. The **crista galli** anchors the falx cerebri, a dural fold.

Example: a fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell (anosmia) or CSF leakage from the nose.
cards.searchQuery: ethmoid bone cribriform plate crista galli

cards.title: Which is the only freely movable bone of the skull (apart from the ossicles)?
cards.body:
Mandible

It articulates with the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). The mandible is the largest and strongest facial bone.

Watch out: the maxillae are fused to the skull and do not move; the hyoid is not part of the skull.
cards.searchQuery: mandible movable skull bone TMJ

cards.title: Which is the largest of the paranasal sinuses?
cards.body:
Maxillary sinus

It lies in the maxilla beside the nasal cavity. The paranasal sinuses are the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary sinuses; they lighten the skull and give voice resonance.

Watch out: the maxillary sinus drains through an opening high on its medial wall, so it drains poorly when you are upright, which contributes to sinus infections.
cards.searchQuery: maxillary sinus largest paranasal sinus

cards.title: How many vertebrae are in the cervical, thoracic and lumbar regions, in that order?
cards.body:
7, 12 and 5

Below the lumbar region are the **sacrum** (five fused vertebrae) and the **coccyx** (three to five fused vertebrae, usually four).

Mnemonic: breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5.
Watch out: this gives 24 separate vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx.
cards.searchQuery: vertebral column regions cervical thoracic lumbar 7 12 5

cards.title: Which cervical vertebra (C2) has a tooth-like dens (odontoid process) around which the atlas rotates?
cards.body:
Axis (C2)

The atlas (C1) pivots on the dens of the axis, allowing you to shake your head "no". The atlas supports the skull and allows nodding "yes" at the atlanto-occipital joint.

Watch out: the atlas has no body or spinous process; its body became the dens of C2 during development.
cards.searchQuery: axis C2 dens odontoid process atlas

cards.title: How many pairs of true (vertebrosternal) ribs are there? Give the number only.
cards.body:
7

Ribs 1 to 7 attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage. Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs (cartilage joins the rib above), and ribs 11 and 12 are **floating ribs** with no anterior attachment.

Example: broken floating ribs are particularly vulnerable because they are not tied to the sternum.
cards.searchQuery: true ribs vertebrosternal 7 pairs floating ribs

cards.title: Which process of the scapula forms the point of the shoulder and articulates with the clavicle?
cards.body:
Acromion

The acromion is the lateral end of the scapular spine. The acromioclavicular (AC) joint forms between the acromion and the clavicle.

Watch out: the **coracoid process** projects anteriorly and anchors the pectoralis minor, short head of biceps and coracobrachialis; the **glenoid cavity** receives the humeral head.
cards.searchQuery: scapula acromion process acromioclavicular joint

cards.title: The radial groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus is the path of which nerve?
cards.body:
Radial nerve

The nerve spirals around the humerus with the deep brachial artery. A mid-shaft humeral fracture can injure it and cause **wrist drop**.

Watch out: the axillary nerve runs near the surgical neck, and the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone").
cards.searchQuery: humerus radial groove radial nerve wrist drop

cards.title: In anatomical position, which forearm bone lies on the thumb (lateral) side?
cards.body:
Radius

The radius is lateral, the ulna medial. The radial head articulates with the capitulum of the humerus and rotates against the ulna during pronation and supination.

Mnemonic: **R**adius = **R**adial side = thumb side (think **r**ight beside the thumb).
cards.searchQuery: radius lateral forearm bone thumb side

cards.title: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured, usually after a fall on an outstretched hand?
cards.body:
Scaphoid

It lies on the thumb side of the proximal row, forming the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. Its blood supply enters distally, so a fracture can lead to **avascular necrosis** of the proximal piece.

Tip: tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a scaphoid fracture even when the first X-ray is normal.
cards.searchQuery: scaphoid fracture carpal bone anatomical snuffbox

cards.title: Which part of the hip bone supports body weight when you sit, via its ischial tuberosity?
cards.body:
Ischium

The hip bone is formed by the fusion of the **ilium**, **ischium** and **pubis**, which meet at the acetabulum. The ilium is the largest, and its crest is the "hip" you feel.

Tip: the pubic bones join at the pubic symphysis, a cartilaginous joint.
cards.searchQuery: ischium ischial tuberosity sitting hip bone

cards.title: Which lower leg bone is lateral, slender and does not bear body weight?
cards.body:
Fibula

The tibia bears the weight. The fibula's distal end forms the lateral malleolus of the ankle and provides muscle attachment.

Watch out: the tibia is the medial and larger of the two bones; the shin you feel at the front is the tibia.
cards.searchQuery: fibula lateral lower leg bone non-weight-bearing

cards.title: What term describes freely movable joints, including all synovial joints?
cards.body:
Diarthrosis

**Synarthroses** are immovable (sutures); **amphiarthroses** are slightly movable (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis); **diarthroses** are freely movable.

Mnemonic: **syn** = together/fixed, **amphi** = both (slightly), **dia** = through/freely.
cards.searchQuery: diarthrosis freely movable joints classification

cards.title: What is the name of the small fluid-filled sac lined by synovial membrane that reduces friction where tendons, muscles or skin rub against bone?
cards.body:
Bursa

Bursae cushion areas of friction around joints such as the shoulder, elbow and knee. Inflammation of a bursa is **bursitis**.

Watch out: a bursa is a closed sac, whereas a tendon sheath is an elongated bursa that wraps a tendon.
cards.searchQuery: bursa bursitis synovial friction

cards.title: Which synovial joint type allows the greatest range of motion, in all planes, and includes the shoulder and hip?
cards.body:
Ball-and-socket joint

This is a multiaxial joint. The shoulder (glenohumeral) is the most mobile joint but the least stable; the hip is deeper and sturdier.

Key idea: more mobility generally means less stability.
cards.searchQuery: ball and socket joint shoulder hip multiaxial

cards.title: What is the term for moving a limb away from the body's midline in the frontal plane, such as raising your arm out to the side?
cards.body:
Abduction

The opposite is **adduction**, moving toward the midline.

Mnemonic: **ab**duction takes a limb **ab**way (like an alien abduction); **ad**duction **ad**ds it back to the body.
cards.searchQuery: abduction adduction movement midline

cards.title: Which synovial joint type, permitting only flexion and extension in one plane, describes the elbow (humeroulnar) joint?
cards.body:
Hinge joint

It is uniaxial. Other examples are the interphalangeal joints; the knee is a modified hinge that also permits slight rotation when flexed.

Tip: compare with the pivot joint (rotation: atlantoaxial) and the ball-and-socket joint (all planes: shoulder, hip).
cards.searchQuery: hinge joint elbow flexion extension uniaxial

cards.title: Which knee ligament prevents the tibia from sliding forward on the femur and is commonly torn in pivoting sports injuries?
cards.body:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)

The ACL runs from the anterior tibia to the posterior femur and also limits hyperextension. The **posterior cruciate ligament** prevents posterior displacement of the tibia.

Example: in the anterior drawer test, a lax ACL lets the tibia slide forward.
cards.searchQuery: anterior cruciate ligament ACL knee tibia anterior displacement

cards.title: Which connective tissue sheath surrounds a bundle (fascicle) of muscle fibers?
cards.body:
Perimysium

The three wrappings are:
- **Endomysium**: around each muscle fiber.
- **Perimysium**: around each fascicle.
- **Epimysium**: around the whole muscle.

Key idea: all three are continuous with the tendon, so force is transmitted from fibers to bone.
cards.searchQuery: perimysium fascicle muscle connective tissue sheath

cards.title: Which organelle of a muscle fiber stores calcium and releases it to trigger contraction?
cards.body:
Sarcoplasmic reticulum

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is the muscle fiber's specialized smooth ER. It releases $\ce{Ca^2+}$ from its **terminal cisternae** when an action potential travels down the T tubules, and pumps it back to end the contraction.

Watch out: the $\ce{Ca^2+}$ is stored in the SR; it is not made in mitochondria.
cards.searchQuery: sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium storage muscle contraction

cards.title: What are the invaginations of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into a muscle fiber?
cards.body:
Transverse (T) tubules

A T tubule with the two adjacent terminal cisternae of the SR forms a **triad**. The action potential in the T tubule signals the SR to release $\ce{Ca^2+}$.

Key idea: T tubules ensure that all sarcomeres contract nearly simultaneously.
cards.searchQuery: T tubules transverse tubules sarcolemma triad

cards.title: What is the term for one motor neuron together with all the muscle fibers it innervates?
cards.body:
Motor unit

When the neuron fires, all of its muscle fibers contract. Small motor units (few fibers per neuron) allow fine control, as in the eye muscles; large ones (hundreds of fibers) are found in muscles like the gastrocnemius.

Key idea: increasing force means recruiting more motor units.
cards.searchQuery: motor unit motor neuron muscle fibers

cards.title: What is the name for a smooth, sustained contraction that occurs when stimuli arrive so fast that the muscle has no time to relax?
cards.body:
Tetanus (fused tetanus)

At lower frequencies the muscle partially relaxes between stimuli (unfused or incomplete tetanus). At high frequency the twitches summate into a smooth plateau of maximal tension.

Watch out: the infection tetanus (Clostridium tetani toxin) is unrelated to the physiological term, though it causes sustained spasm.
cards.searchQuery: fused tetanus muscle contraction frequency summation

cards.title: What type of contraction develops tension without changing muscle length, as when you hold a heavy book at a fixed position?
cards.body:
Isometric contraction

The cross-bridges generate force, but the load is too great or the object is fixed, so the muscle does not shorten.

Watch out: in an **isotonic** contraction the muscle changes length while tension stays roughly constant. Isotonic contractions can be concentric or eccentric.
cards.searchQuery: isometric contraction tension no change in length

cards.title: What term describes a contraction in which the muscle lengthens while producing tension, such as when you lower a weight slowly?
cards.body:
Eccentric contraction

In a **concentric** contraction the muscle shortens (lifting the weight). Eccentric contractions act as a brake and are associated with more delayed-onset muscle soreness.

Example: walking downhill uses eccentric contractions of the quadriceps.
cards.searchQuery: eccentric contraction muscle lengthens under tension

cards.title: Which attachment of a muscle is the more movable one, usually pulled toward the less movable origin when the muscle contracts?
cards.body:
Insertion

The **origin** is the less movable (usually proximal) attachment. The insertion is the attachment on the bone that moves.

Example: the biceps brachii originates on the scapula and inserts on the radius.
Watch out: the roles can change with posture; in a pull-up the insertion is relatively fixed.
cards.searchQuery: muscle origin insertion movable attachment

cards.title: What is the name for a muscle that opposes the action of the prime mover (agonist)?
cards.body:
Antagonist

The antagonist relaxes or lengthens to allow the prime mover to act, giving smooth, controlled movements. Synergists assist the prime mover, and fixators stabilize a joint or origin.

Example: when the biceps flexes the elbow (prime mover), the triceps is the antagonist.
cards.searchQuery: antagonist muscle prime mover agonist synergist

cards.title: The biceps brachii pulls on the forearm between the elbow (fulcrum) and the hand (load). What class of lever is this?
cards.body:
Third-class lever

In a third-class lever the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. It is the most common lever type in the body and favors speed and range of motion over force.

Watch out: in a first-class lever the fulcrum lies in the middle (nodding the head); in a second-class lever the load lies in the middle (standing on tiptoe).
cards.searchQuery: third class lever biceps elbow effort between fulcrum load

cards.title: Which rounded shoulder muscle, innervated by the axillary nerve, is a common site for intramuscular injections and abducts the arm?
cards.body:
Deltoid

Its middle fibers abduct the arm after the supraspinatus has initiated the first 15 degrees. Its anterior fibers flex and its posterior fibers extend the arm.

Watch out: a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus can damage the axillary nerve and cause deltoid weakness.
cards.searchQuery: deltoid muscle axillary nerve arm abduction

cards.title: Which four muscles make up the rotator cuff that stabilizes the shoulder joint?
cards.body:
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis

The mnemonic is **SITS**. Their tendons blend with the glenohumeral joint capsule and hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity.

Watch out: the supraspinatus tendon is the most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon because it passes under the acromion.
cards.searchQuery: rotator cuff muscles SITS shoulder stabilize

cards.title: Which anterior arm muscle, innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve, flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm?
cards.body:
Biceps brachii

It has two heads at the shoulder (long and short) and inserts on the radial tuberosity. It is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed.

Watch out: the **brachialis**, deep to the biceps, is the main elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.
cards.searchQuery: biceps brachii musculocutaneous nerve elbow flexion supination

cards.title: Which anterior abdominal muscle, with tendinous intersections giving a "six-pack" look, flexes the trunk?
cards.body:
Rectus abdominis

It runs vertically on each side of the **linea alba**. The tendinous intersections divide it into segments. It also compresses the abdomen.

Watch out: the lateral abdominal wall has three layers (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis); the rectus is the long, strap-like anterior muscle.
cards.searchQuery: rectus abdominis trunk flexion tendinous intersections

cards.title: Which muscle is the largest in the body and the chief extensor of the thigh at the hip, innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve?
cards.body:
Gluteus maximus

It extends the thigh powerfully during climbing, running and rising from a seated position, and it also laterally rotates the thigh.

Watch out: the gluteus medius, not the maximus, abducts the thigh and keeps the pelvis level during walking.
cards.searchQuery: gluteus maximus largest muscle hip extension

cards.title: Which anterior thigh muscle group, innervated by the femoral nerve, extends the knee?
cards.body:
Quadriceps femoris

It has four parts: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius. They share the **quadriceps tendon**, which includes the patella and continues as the patellar ligament.

Tip: only the rectus femoris also flexes the thigh at the hip, because it crosses both joints.
cards.searchQuery: quadriceps femoris femoral nerve knee extension

cards.title: Which neck muscle, innervated by the accessory nerve (CN XI), turns the head to the opposite side when one side contracts?
cards.body:
Sternocleidomastoid

It runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. When both sides contract together they flex the neck.

Watch out: contraction of the right sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the left. Unilateral shortening causes torticollis (wry neck).
cards.searchQuery: sternocleidomastoid muscle accessory nerve head rotation

cards.title: Which tendon attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus, enabling plantar flexion?
cards.body:
Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon

It is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the foot, as in standing on tiptoe or push-off in walking.

Watch out: only the gastrocnemius also crosses the knee and flexes it; the soleus acts at the ankle only.
cards.searchQuery: Achilles calcaneal tendon gastrocnemius soleus plantar flexion
